[PAPER_0027, relevance_score=0.352] We will test the competing perceptual and behavioral confirmation hypotheses within the context of day-to-day behavioral relationship expectations using lagged panel analyses (see Figure 1, for a visual depiction). Consistent with perceptual confirmation, people who expect more positive behaviors from the partner might selectively notice any positive behaviors that the partner does to a greater extent than those who expect few behaviors. In turn, their perceptions of their partner's behaviors may largely align with their expectations, independently of what their partner actually did or did not do for them (dotted line).

[PAPER_0043, relevance_score=0.420] The Present Research

The present research provides the most direct test to date of these five different hypotheses about how relationship expectations may shape relationship outcomes. Previous studies have explored these theoretical models relatively separately, using different samples, study designs, measures, and statistical approaches. We sought to extend this work by testing all five models using the same data in a way that would allow us to compare the strength of evidence for each. We examined the mutual influence of expectations and perceptions of these behaviors as well as relationship quality over time using a dynamical systems approach.
items.paper_content_summary: The paper tests five models, including expectations predicting perceptions, relationship quality predicting expectations, expectations predicting relationship quality, and expectations moderating the association between perceived behaviors and quality. It distinguishes perceptual from behavioral confirmation as competing explanations for the expectations–perceptions association. [PAPER_0043] [PAPER_0027] [PAPER_0028] [PAPER_0042] [PAPER_0096]

[PAPER_0023, relevance_score=0.254] For example, in a lab study on interrogation (Kassin et al., 2003), participants in the role of "interrogator" were randomly assigned to be told that statistically, their suspect was either probably guilty (guilty expectations) or probably innocent (innocent expectations). Interrogators with guilty expectations conducted more aggressive interrogations, which led their suspects to act in ways that made them appear guiltier to outside observers. Expectations about a partner's relationship behaviors may similarly be a self-fulfilling prophecy whereby partners tend to live up to the expectations set for them.

[PAPER_0044, relevance_score=0.321] Dynamical systems is a metatheoretical perspective that assumes that every construct of interest ebbs and flows over time in meaningful ways (Butner et al., 2005). Within this framework, cyclical change is treated as signal rather than noise.

Each variable is treated as both a predictor and an outcome variable, so as to directly capture the ways that the variables mutually push and pull each other over time. This novel conceptualization of the research question allows us to directly test four of the theoretical models of interest within a single cross-lagged panel model (see Figure 4).

[PAPER_0080, relevance_score=0.283] Expectations as a Potential Moderator

As in Study 1, we next tested whether expectations moderated the association between perceived partner behaviors and relationship quality (as implied by the suffocation model). In these modified lagged panel models, this week's perceived behaviors were removed as a dependent measure, and last week's perceived behaviors were replaced with this week's perceived behaviors as a predictor. Further, we added an interaction term between last week's expected behaviors and this week's perceived behaviors predicting this week's relationship quality. We tested these models for both positive and negative behaviors.

[PAPER_0080, relevance_score=0.346] Expectations as a Potential Moderator

As in Study 1, we next tested whether expectations moderated the association between perceived partner behaviors and relationship quality (as implied by the suffocation model). In these modified lagged panel models, this week's perceived behaviors were removed as a dependent measure, and last week's perceived behaviors were replaced with this week's perceived behaviors as a predictor. Further, we added an interaction term between last week's expected behaviors and this week's perceived behaviors predicting this week's relationship quality. We tested these models for both positive and negative behaviors.

[PREREG_0010, relevance_score=0.450] q17.question: We will use a dynamical systems approach to examine competing ideas about how relationship expectations, perceptions of partner's behaviours, and relationship quality (i.e., satisfaction, commitment, gratitude, and trust) influence each other from week to week during a relationship. All analyses will be two-level multilevel models conducted using the lme4 package (Bates, 2015) to account for the data's nested structure. The three key weekly variables used in the primary model will be: 1. Perceived Behaviours (positive and negative) 2.

[PREREG_0011, relevance_score=0.349] Perceived Behaviours (positive and negative) 2. Forecasted Behaviours (positive and negative) 3. Relationship Quality (i.e., satisfaction, commitment, gratitude, and trust)

Positive versus negative behaviors will be tested in separate models, each including a separate relationship quality indicator. For example, one model will examine positive perceived behaviors, positive forecasted behaviors, and satisfaction from week to week.

[PREREG_0012, relevance_score=0.443] In total, we will conduct eight cross-lagged panel models in which each construct of interest - perceived behaviours, expected behaviours, and relationship quality - is modelled simultaneously as a predictor and as an outcome variable. "Last week" versions of each variable will be used as predictors (Time 1) and "this week" versions will be used as outcome variables (Time 2). Data will be restructured so that each of the three outcome variables - perceived behaviours, expected behaviours, and relationship quality at Time 2 - are combined into a single dependent variable column.

[PREREG_0013, relevance_score=0.427] Overall, each participant will have up to 12 rows in the data set: one for each dependent measure on each of the 4 weeks (Week 1 will be excluded because it will be missing "last week" variables). Three new dummy columns will be created to indicate which rows correspond to which DVs. The model will have a total of 12 predictors: each of the three dummy columns, plus each of the three dummy columns multiplied by each of the three Time 1 predictors. This analysis strategy will allow us to model all time change effects simultaneously in one model.
